what: Buenaventura is Peru’s largest precious metals miner. It operates gold, silver, copper, lead and zinc mines in Peru, holds a substantial minority stake in the enormous Cerro Verde copper mine, and owns an interest in power transmission and other industrial assets.
customers: Metal traders, smelters and refiners who buy its concentrate and bullion, with pricing set by international metal markets.
money: Gold, silver, zinc and lead from its own operated mines in Peru.
Its share of earnings from the Cerro Verde copper mine and other investments.
moat: Buenaventura has operated in Peru for generations, which matters enormously in a country where community relations, water rights and local politics determine whether a mine can operate at all. Its stake in Cerro Verde — one of the world’s larger copper mines, operated by Freeport — provides copper exposure without the operating burden.
risks: Peru carries real political and social risk: community protests have shut down major mines, and governments have changed mining tax and royalty policy repeatedly.
Revenue depends entirely on metal prices, which the company does not control, and swung from $824.8M in 2022 to $1.7B in 2025.
Only six analysts cover the stock, and their $36.83 average against a $21.23 price is a 74% gap reflecting very different views on Peru risk.
Mine lives are finite, so reserves must be replaced through exploration or acquisition simply to maintain production.
Debt of $693.3M against $478.4M of cash is manageable but the earnings are volatile enough to matter.
opportunities: Trailing net income of $1.1B on $2.3B of revenue, with free cash flow of $858.9M.
The shares trade at about 4.7 times earnings, 4.0 times EV/EBITDA and 6.3 times free cash flow — very low multiples.
The Cerro Verde stake gives copper exposure through a world-class, long-life asset operated by someone else.
Generations of operating experience in Peru is a genuine advantage in a country where social licence determines whether mines run.
Operating leverage is high: metal price increases flow almost entirely to profit against a largely fixed cost base.
watch: Production volumes by metal and all-in costs. Metal prices are outside anyone’s control; volumes and costs are what management affects and what determines whether high prices convert to cash.
view: Buenaventura offers an unusual combination: a Peruvian precious metals miner at 4.7 times earnings that also happens to own a meaningful stake in one of the world’s larger copper mines, operated by Freeport. The Cerro Verde interest is the part I find most attractive, because it provides exposure to a world-class, long-life copper asset without Buenaventura bearing the operating burden — it simply receives its share of the earnings.

The operated mines are a more conventional proposition and a more volatile one. Revenue swung from $825 million in 2022 to $1.7 billion in 2025, with trailing revenue of $2.3 billion and trailing net income of $1.1 billion. Nothing fundamental changed; metal prices rose, and against a largely fixed cost base, almost all of it reached the bottom line. The same leverage works in reverse, which is why a 4.7 times multiple on peak earnings is not the bargain it appears.

The reason the shares trade this cheaply is Peru, and the risk is specific rather than vague. Community protests have shut down major Peruvian mines for extended periods, water rights disputes are common, and successive governments have changed mining taxation and royalties. What partly offsets this is Buenaventura’s history: it has operated in Peru for generations and understands the social and political terrain far better than a foreign entrant. In mining, social licence is a real asset even though it appears on no balance sheet.

So the honest framing is that this is genuinely cheap, genuinely leveraged to metal prices, and genuinely exposed to a jurisdiction that has interrupted mines before. Six analysts averaging 74% above the price tells you how differently people weigh that last point. I would want to know production volumes and all-in costs by mine rather than the consolidated figures, because the metal price is outside anyone’s control and costs are the only thing that determines whether a strong price survives the journey to cash.
bull: Metal prices hold, high operating leverage converts them to cash, and the Cerro Verde copper stake plus generations of Peruvian experience justify far more than 4.7 times earnings.
bear: Community protests or a government policy change interrupts production, metal prices fall and the leverage reverses, and the Peru discount proves permanent.
